articles.title: Apple acknowledges iPhone Duo display ‘issue’ after reports of cracked screens
articles.summary: Following reports of iPhone Duos with cracked and broken inside screens, often showing a bright line running from the center to the right side, Apple says in a statement to Bloomberg and 9to5Mac that it's aware of "an issue impacting the inner display" on a "small number of iPhone Duo units." If…
body: Apple says a ‘small number’ of iPhone Duos have shown the cracked inner screen problem and that owners should contact AppleCare.

Shortly after launch, iPhone Duo users started reporting similar issues where the hinge would tighten, and opening the device caused a crack and the distinctive bright lines on the display. One user in Australia said that an Apple Store replaced their unit “on the spot.”

This weekend, iFixit published its teardown of the phone and gave its perspective on why some phones might be cracking. Where the damage has been happening, iFixit shows how the foldable screen might be pushing against a center bar.

The Verge has contacted Apple about the reports, but has not received an on-the-record response about the issues with these new phones. They’re some of the first devices to launch after new CEO John Ternus took over from Tim Cook.

articles.title: Some iPhone Duo screens are already failing
articles.summary: The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple's first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn't going great.
body: The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin.

Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo's screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO filing reveals rapid revenue gains and even larger losses
articles.summary: Market debut of AI company behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of the AI boom’s financial viability. Anthropic has publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history.
body: Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT, confidentially filed with US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June.

“We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the company’s investor prospectus reads. Anthropic researchers and executives have trumpeted the transformative power of AI while simultaneously warning of its potential to cause human extinction.

A leader in the race to create powerful artificial intelligence models and a bellwether of the American AI boom, Anthropic’s chatbot Claude is its flagship product, which offers text generation features as well as advanced coding and cybersecurity capabilities. CEO Dario Amodei founded the company after quitting OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT.

Anthropic’s audited filings will offer the first public glimpse of its financial health, which have been the object of intense speculation in recent months as questions of a potential AI bubble swirl.

articles.title: F1 in Texas: The American race that fans love to attend
articles.summary: Audi provided flights from Washington, DC, to Austin, Texas, and accommodation so Ars could attend the US Grand Prix. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. AUSTIN, Texas—Formula 1 returned to US shores this weekend with its annual visit to the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas.
body: Unlike Miami or Las Vegas, which race on temporary street circuits, COTA is a permanent race track with plenty of run-off areas instead of concrete walls. Designed by motorcycle racer Kevin Schwanz—Herman Tilke’s company did only the buildings and infrastructure, contrary to popular belief—the track combines a mix of corner speeds with challenging turn sequences, a few heavy braking zones, and plenty of elevation changes.

It’s a place Ars knows rather intimately by now. We’ve driven it in everything from an Audi TT-S to a Corvette ZR1 to a bicycle, and that’s just in the real world. Over the years, we’ve been there for F1 to learn about how the sport puts together its broadcasts, how Pirelli designs its tires, and how various tech partners help teams manage their data and strategies. We even saw the race through a neophyte’s eyes. And that’s just F1—we’ve logged many hours there with the World Endurance Championship and IMSA for the Lone Star Le Mans races in sweaty September.

articles.title: Tesla gave up the EV crown. Now it wants to win the autonomy race.
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s “flying” Roadster jumped and flipped through the air this month in a stunt that went viral around the world. But his bigger bet is on changing the way Tesla makes money—and the wider car industry is scrambling to catch up.
body: Five days after the spectacle, made possible by compressed-gas thrusters developed by Musk’s SpaceX, he revealed the companies were exploring a merger that could accelerate his push into autonomous driving.

At stake is more than a technological race. Car groups, already grappling with growing Chinese competition, are seeking to move beyond a business model centered on vehicle sales towards one that also generates recurring revenues from software and AI-powered services.

“Automakers are starting to look in the mirror and the software piece is what they are all looking at as the golden goose, because the margins are so high,” said Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner at merchant bank Yorkville Ives.

Even with Tesla’s strategic shift in recent years, its car business remains a crucial cash cow for the group, where it generates 75 percent of total revenues and will be pivotal for the heavy spending Tesla will need to make in AI to compete with its Big Tech rivals.

articles.title: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing
articles.summary: The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it's updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site.
body: Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.

The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. On the retailer’s website, an item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart. Using Meta’s Muse, The Verge was able to instruct the AI agent to continuously re-add The RealReal listings in a shopping cart as soon as the 20-minute hold had expired, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing products for hours or longer.

After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge ’s story. The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out, Friang said. Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages, Friang said, adding that the company will continue to strengthen protections as AI-powered online shopping evolves.
points: The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it's updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site.

articles.title: Highway thieves are spoofing GPS to steal millions in data center-bound cargo
articles.summary: Highway thieves are using sophisticated digital tactics that investigators worry make it easy to rob trucks carrying millions in expensive data center equipment. NBC News spoke to “several industry leaders, consultants, and investigators advising law enforcement” offices probing the biggest thefts…
body: Equipment commonly targeted includes “servers, fiber-optic cables, computer memory chips, copper wires, and bitcoin mining machines,” NBC News reported.

Some trailers hit seem to be carrying only data center equipment, like two stolen freights found in Illinois. The Cook County Sheriff’s Office estimated those contained $300,000 worth of copper wire spools and about $1 million in “custom-made data center modular power solutions equipment,” NBC News reported. Other trucks impacted were carrying additional freight, like a Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department case where “data center cooling equipment” bound for Deepcool AI was recovered among nicotine pouches, televisions, shoes, printers, speakers, and skin care cosmetics. Experts worry that means Americans may be broadly harmed by the thefts, not just the AI industry.

While some stolen goods have been recovered, in two of the largest thefts that NBC News found, none of the equipment was found, and off-duty cops hired to escort the shipments were targeted in hit-and-runs.

The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) also says businesses and critical infrastructure must use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats, raising alarm that artificial intelligence is enabling more dangerous threats than ever.

articles.title: Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing
articles.summary: Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions.
body: From conscious AI and ‘catastrophic’ risk to unusual corporate structures and executive perks.

Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Admittedly, it is at the lower end of the Big Tech scale, but it is still a tidy sum.

And that’s not all. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055.
The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Claude AI model accessed Georgia voter data in US
articles.summary: Latest example of unauthorised behaviour shows AI model bypassed paywall to access data as part of statistics project. Anthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis songs to train AI models.
body: Anthropic’s Claude model accessed voter data in the US state of Georgia, the AI company has confirmed, in the latest example of unauthorised behaviour by the technology.

The AI model managed to bypass a paywall to reach data that is publicly available but is typically accessible only after paying a fee. Claude accessed aggregate vote counts as part of a statistics project at Anthropic, which is preparing for a $1.5tn (£1.1tn) flotation.
“Claude did not access the state’s voter registration system, change any voting records, or pull any individual voter records,” Anthropic said.

Anthropic said the AI found a loophole in an old version of the state agency’s website, discovering that it issued a digital entry pass – an “access token” – to visitors. It then requested a token and gained access to the information.

articles.title: The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans
articles.summary: Two US senators say the Trump administration is breaking the law by withholding the FISA court decision while it presses Congress to renew America’s most sweeping surveillance program.
body: Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.

The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.
points: Two US senators say the Trump administration is breaking the law by withholding the FISA court decision while it presses Congress to renew America’s most sweeping surveillance program.
